topics.title: Real numbers and functions
topics.content:
Real numbers are the foundation of mathematical analysis. They possess the properties of an ordered field and completeness (the least upper bound axiom).

Basic properties:
  • Ordered: for any two numbers we can say which is greater.
  • Completeness: any non‑empty set bounded above has a least upper bound.
Absolute value:

|a| = a if a ≥ 0, and |a| = -a if a < 0. Properties: |ab| = |a||b|, |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b| (triangle inequality).

Number sets:
  • Open interval (a,b) = {x | a < x < b}
  • Closed interval [a,b] = {x | a ≤ x ≤ b}
  • Neighbourhood of a point a – interval (a-ε, a+ε).
Concept of a function:

A function f: X → Y assigns to each element x∈X a unique element y∈Y. Ways of definition: analytic (formula), graphic, tabular. Domain D(f) – the set of admissible x, range E(f) – the set of all values taken by y.

Basic elementary functions:
  • Power: y = x^a
  • Exponential: y = a^x (a>0, a≠1)
  • Logarithmic: y = log_a x
  • Trigonometric: sin x, cos x, tan x, cot x
  • Inverse trigonometric: arcsin x, arccos x, arctan x, arccot x

Their properties: graphs, periodicity (for trigonometric functions), even/odd parity.

topics.title: Limit of a numerical sequence
topics.content:
A sequence {x_n} has limit a if for every ε > 0 there exists an index N(ε) such that for all n > N we have |x_n - a| < ε. Notation: lim x_n = a.

Properties of convergent sequences:
  • The limit is unique.
  • A convergent sequence is bounded.
  • Algebra of limits: lim (x_n ± y_n) = lim x_n ± lim y_n, lim (x_n·y_n) = lim x_n · lim y_n, lim (x_n/y_n) = lim x_n / lim y_n (provided lim y_n ≠ 0).
Infinitesimal and infinitely large sequences:
  • A sequence α_n → 0 is called infinitesimal.
  • If |x_n| → ∞, the sequence is infinitely large.
Criteria for existence of a limit:
  • Weierstrass theorem: a monotone bounded sequence converges.
  • The number e = lim (1 + 1/n)^n.

Relation with infinitesimals: x_n → a ⇔ x_n - a → 0.

topics.title: Limit of a function
topics.content:
Cauchy definition (ε-δ):

A number L is called the limit of f(x) as x → a if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that for all x satisfying 0 < |x - a| < δ we have |f(x) - L| < ε.

Heine definition (in terms of sequences):

lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if for every sequence {x_n} → a (x_n ≠ a) the corresponding sequence {f(x_n)} → L.

One‑sided limits:
  • Left‑hand limit: x → a⁻
  • Right‑hand limit: x → a⁺
Properties of limits:
  • Uniqueness.
  • Local boundedness of a function that has a finite limit.
  • Arithmetic operations: limit of sum, product, quotient (if denominator ≠ 0).
  • Limit of a composition.
Remarkable limits:
  • lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1
  • lim_{x→∞} (1 + 1/x)^x = e
Equivalent functions as x→0:
  • sin x ∼ x
  • tan x ∼ x
  • arcsin x ∼ x
  • arctan x ∼ x
  • ln(1+x) ∼ x
  • e^x - 1 ∼ x
  • (1+x)^α - 1 ∼ αx
Resolving indeterminate forms:

types 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0. They are reduced to 0/0 or ∞/∞ by logarithmic or algebraic transformations.

topics.title: Continuity of a function
topics.content:
A function f is continuous at point a if lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a). This means three conditions hold:

  • f is defined at a;
  • the finite limit as x→a exists;
  • the limit equals the function value.
Left‑hand and right‑hand continuity:

Analogous to one‑sided limits.

Discontinuities and their classification:
  1. Removable discontinuity: lim f(x) exists but is not equal to f(a) (or f(a) is undefined).
  2. Jump discontinuity (first kind): one‑sided limits are finite but not equal.
  3. Discontinuity of the second kind: at least one one‑sided limit is infinite or does not exist.
Properties of continuous functions:
  • The sum, product, and quotient (with non‑zero denominator) of continuous functions are continuous.
  • The composition of continuous functions is continuous.
  • All elementary functions are continuous on their domains.

topics.title: Properties of continuous functions on a closed interval
topics.content:
Weierstrass theorem:

If a function f is continuous on [a,b], then it is bounded on that interval and attains its supremum and infimum, i.e., there exist points x₁, x₂ ∈ [a,b] such that f(x₁) = max f, f(x₂) = min f.

Cauchy intermediate value theorem:

If f is continuous on [a,b] and C is a number between f(a) and f(b), then there exists a point c ∈ (a,b) such that f(c) = C.

Corollary:

If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (f(a)·f(b) < 0), then the equation f(x) = 0 has at least one root in the interval (a,b).

topics.title: Derivative of a function
topics.content:
Definition:

The derivative of f at point x0 is the limit
f'(x0) = lim_{Δx→0} (f(x0+Δx) - f(x0)) / Δx,
provided the limit exists. The function is then called differentiable at x0.

Geometric meaning:

f'(x0) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph y = f(x) at the point (x0, f(x0)).

Physical meaning:

instantaneous rate of change.

Necessary condition for differentiability:

the function must be continuous at the point.

Differentiation rules:
  • (c)' = 0
  • (u ± v)' = u' ± v'
  • (uv)' = u'v + uv'
  • (u/v)' = (u'v - uv') / v² (v ≠ 0)
  • Chain rule: (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x))·g'(x)
  • Derivative of inverse function: (f^{-1})'(y) = 1 / f'(x), where y = f(x).
Table of derivatives of basic functions:
  • (x^n)' = n x^{n-1}
  • (e^x)' = e^x
  • (a^x)' = a^x ln a
  • (ln x)' = 1/x
  • (sin x)' = cos x
  • (cos x)' = -sin x
  • (tan x)' = 1/cos² x
  • (cot x)' = -1/sin² x
  • (arcsin x)' = 1/√(1-x²)
  • (arccos x)' = -1/√(1-x²)
  • (arctan x)' = 1/(1+x²)
  • (arccot x)' = -1/(1+x²)
Logarithmic differentiation:

Convenient for functions of the form y = u^v or products of many factors: take ln y = v ln u, then differentiate.

topics.title: Differential of a function
topics.content:
Definition:

The differential of y = f(x) at x0 is the principal linear part of the increment:
dy = f'(x0) dx, where dx = Δx.

Geometric meaning:

dy is the increment of the ordinate of the tangent line.

Invariance of the first differential:

dy = f'(u) du, where u can be either an independent variable or a function.

Application to approximate calculations:

f(x0 + Δx) ≈ f(x0) + f'(x0) Δx.

Higher order differentials:

d²y = f''(x) dx² (assuming x is an independent variable). The form changes under a change of variable.

topics.title: Higher order derivatives
topics.content:
Definition:

The derivative of order n is defined recursively:
f^{(n)}(x) = (f^{(n-1)}(x))'.
Notation: f''(x), f'''(x), f^{(4)}(x), etc.

Physical meaning of the second derivative:

acceleration (derivative of velocity).

Leibniz rule

for the derivative of a product of two functions:
(uv)^{(n)} = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C_n^k u^{(k)} v^{(n-k)},
where C_n^k are binomial coefficients.

Applications:

investigation of functions (convexity, inflection points), Taylor series.

topics.title: Mean value theorems for differentiable functions
topics.content:
Rolle's theorem:

If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a) = f(b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that f'(c) = 0. Geometrically, there is a point with a horizontal tangent.

Lagrange's theorem (finite increments formula):

If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that
f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a).

Corollaries:
  • If f'(x) = 0 on an interval, then f is constant.
  • If f'(x) > 0 (f'(x) < 0) on an interval, then f is increasing (decreasing).
Cauchy's theorem (generalised):

If f and g are continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a,b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that
(f(b)-f(a))/(g(b)-g(a)) = f'(c)/g'(c).

topics.title: Investigating functions using the derivative
topics.content:
Monotonicity:
  • If f'(x) > 0 on an interval, the function is increasing.
  • If f'(x) < 0 on an interval, the function is decreasing.
Extrema:
  • Necessary condition: if x0 is a point of local extremum of a differentiable function, then f'(x0) = 0 (stationary point).
  • Sufficient conditions:
    • If the first derivative changes sign from plus to minus – maximum; from minus to plus – minimum.
    • Using the second derivative: if f''(x0) > 0 – minimum; if f''(x0) < 0 – maximum; if f''(x0) = 0 – further investigation is needed.
Convexity and inflection points:
  • If f''(x) > 0 on an interval, the graph is convex downward (concave up).
  • If f''(x) < 0, the graph is convex upward (concave down).
  • An inflection point is where f''(x) changes sign (and f''(x0)=0 or does not exist).
Asymptotes:
  • Vertical: x = a, if lim_{x→a} f(x) = ∞.
  • Oblique: y = kx + b, where k = lim_{x→±∞} f(x)/x, b = lim_{x→±∞} (f(x) - kx).
General scheme for function analysis:
  1. Domain, discontinuities, parity, periodicity.
  2. Find the derivative, stationary points, intervals of monotonicity and extrema.
  3. Second derivative, intervals of convexity, inflection points.
  4. Asymptotes.
  5. Table of values, plot the graph.

topics.title: L'Hôpital's rule
topics.content:
Resolving indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞.

If f and g are differentiable in a punctured neighbourhood of a, g'(x) ≠ 0, and lim_{x→a} f(x) = lim_{x→a} g(x) = 0 (or ∞), then
lim_{x→a} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→a} f'(x)/g'(x),
provided the latter limit exists (finite or infinite).

Can be applied repeatedly

if the indeterminate form persists after the first differentiation.

Other indeterminate forms

(0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰) are reduced to 0/0 or ∞/∞ by transformations:

  • 0·∞ → rewrite as 0/(1/∞) or ∞/(1/0).
  • ∞-∞ → bring to a common denominator or multiply by the conjugate.
  • 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ → use logarithmic transformation: lim u^v = e^{lim v ln u}.

topics.title: Taylor's formula
topics.content:
Taylor's formula with Peano remainder:

If f has derivatives up to order n at x0, then
f(x) = f(x0) + f'(x0)(x-x0)/1! + ... + f^{(n)}(x0)(x-x0)^n/n! + o((x-x0)^n).

Lagrange remainder:

R_n(x) = f^{(n+1)}(ξ)(x-x0)^{n+1}/(n+1)!, where ξ lies between x and x0.

Maclaurin series

special case when x0 = 0.

Expansions of basic functions:
  • e^x = Σ x^n/n!
  • sin x = Σ (-1)^n x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!
  • cos x = Σ (-1)^n x^{2n}/(2n)!
  • ln(1+x) = Σ (-1)^{n-1} x^n/n, |x|<1
  • (1+x)^α = 1 + αx + α(α-1)x²/2! + ... (binomial series)
Applications:
  • Approximate calculation of function values.
  • Evaluation of limits.
  • Studying the behaviour of a function near a point.

topics.title: Antiderivative and indefinite integral
topics.content:
Antiderivative:

A function F is called an antiderivative of f on an interval if F'(x) = f(x) for all x in that interval.

Property:

any two antiderivatives differ by a constant.

Indefinite integral:

∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

Linearity:

∫ (αf(x) + βg(x)) dx = α∫ f(x) dx + β∫ g(x) dx.

Table of basic integrals:
  • ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + C (n ≠ -1)
  • ∫ dx/x = ln|x| + C
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C
  • ∫ a^x dx = a^x / ln a + C
  • ∫ sin x dx = -cos x + C
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
  • ∫ dx/cos²x = tan x + C
  • ∫ dx/sin²x = -cot x + C
  • ∫ dx/√(1-x²) = arcsin x + C
  • ∫ dx/(1+x²) = arctan x + C

topics.title: Substitution method in indefinite integrals
topics.content:
Substitution formula:

If x = φ(t) is a differentiable function, then
∫ f(x) dx = ∫ f(φ(t)) φ'(t) dt.
After integration, return to the variable x.

Reverse substitution:

∫ f(φ(x)) φ'(x) dx = ∫ f(t) dt, where t = φ(x).

Examples:
  • Linear substitution: ∫ (ax+b)^n dx = 1/a * ∫ t^n dt (t = ax+b).
  • Substitution under the differential sign: ∫ f(φ(x)) φ'(x) dx = ∫ f(t) dt.
  • Trigonometric substitutions for integrals of the form ∫ R(x, √(a²-x²)) dx: x = a sin t, √(a²-x²) = a cos t.

topics.title: Integration by parts
topics.content:
Formula:

∫ u dv = u v - ∫ v du.

Used for

integrals of the form ∫ P(x) e^{ax} dx, ∫ P(x) sin(ax) dx, ∫ P(x) cos(ax) dx, ∫ e^{ax} sin(bx) dx, ∫ ln x dx, ∫ arctan x dx, etc.

Examples:
  • ∫ x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx → du = dx, v = e^x → = x e^x - ∫ e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C.
  • ∫ x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx → du = dx, v = -cos x → = -x cos x + ∫ cos x dx = -x cos x + sin x + C.
  • ∫ ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx → du = dx/x, v = x → = x ln x - ∫ dx = x ln x - x + C.
  • ∫ e^x sin x dx (cyclic): after two integrations we obtain an equation for the integral.

topics.title: Integration of rational functions
topics.content:
A rational function is a quotient of polynomials P(x)/Q(x).

If deg P ≥ deg Q

perform division to obtain a polynomial (the integer part) plus a proper fraction.

Proper fraction

is decomposed into a sum of partial fractions:

  • A/(x-a)^k – for real roots;
  • (Mx+N)/(x²+px+q)^l – for quadratic factors with negative discriminant.
Method of undetermined coefficients:

write the sum with unknown coefficients, bring to a common denominator, and equate coefficients for like powers of x.

Integration of elementary fractions:
  • ∫ A/(x-a) dx = A ln|x-a| + C
  • ∫ A/(x-a)^k dx = A/( (1-k)(x-a)^{k-1} ) + C (k>1)
  • ∫ (Mx+N)/(x²+px+q) dx – by completing the square in the denominator it reduces to a logarithm and an arctangent.
Ostrogradsky's method

allows to extract the rational part of an integral without decomposing into partial fractions (used for multiple roots).

topics.title: Integration of trigonometric expressions
topics.content:
Integrals of the form ∫ R(sin x, cos x) dx, where R is a rational function.

Universal substitution t = tan(x/2):

sin x = 2t/(1+t²), cos x = (1-t²)/(1+t²), dx = 2 dt/(1+t²). This reduces the integral to an integral of a rational function.

Special cases:
  • If R(-sin x, cos x) = -R(sin x, cos x) (odd in sin), substitute t = cos x.
  • If R(sin x, -cos x) = -R(sin x, cos x) (odd in cos), substitute t = sin x.
  • If R(-sin x, -cos x) = R(sin x, cos x) (even), substitute t = tan x.
Integrals of the form ∫ sin^m x cos^n x dx:
  • If m is odd: sin^m x = sin^{m-1} x · sin x, substitute t = cos x.
  • If n is odd: substitute t = sin x.
  • If both m and n are even: use power‑reducing formulas: sin²x = (1-cos2x)/2, cos²x = (1+cos2x)/2.

Also use trigonometric identities (sin x cos x = ½ sin 2x, product‑to‑sum formulas).

topics.title: Integration of irrational functions
topics.content:
Integrals of the form ∫ R(x, √(ax+b)) dx

are reduced to rational integrals by the substitution t = √(ax+b). Then x = (t²-b)/a, dx = 2t/a dt.

Integrals of the form ∫ R(x, √(ax²+bx+c)) dx

require Euler substitutions or trigonometric/hyperbolic substitutions depending on the sign of a and the discriminant.

  • If a > 0, use √(ax²+bx+c) = t ± x√a.
  • If c > 0, use √(ax²+bx+c) = xt ± √c.
  • Trigonometric substitutions:
    • For √(a²-x²): x = a sin t (or a cos t).
    • For √(a²+x²): x = a tan t.
    • For √(x²-a²): x = a sec t.
Integrals of differential binomials

∫ x^m (a + b x^n)^p dx, where m, n, p are rational numbers. They are integrable in elementary functions in three cases (Chebyshev conditions):

  1. p is an integer.
  2. (m+1)/n is an integer.
  3. (m+1)/n + p is an integer.

topics.title: Riemann definite integral
topics.content:
Area of a curvilinear trapezoid:

the area under the graph of y = f(x) ≥ 0 on [a,b] is found as the limit of integral sums.

Definition:

Partition the interval [a,b] by points a = x0 < x1 < ... < xn = b, and choose a point ξ_i on each subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i]. Form the integral sum Σ f(ξ_i) Δx_i. If, as the mesh (max Δx_i) tends to 0, the limit exists and is independent of the choice of partition and points ξ_i, it is called the definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx.

Classes of integrable functions:

continuous, piecewise continuous (with a finite number of discontinuities), monotone functions.

Properties:
  • Linearity: ∫ (αf+βg) = α∫ f + β∫ g.
  • Additivity with respect to the interval: ∫_a^b f = ∫_a^c f + ∫_c^b f.
  • Monotonicity: if f ≤ g, then ∫ f ≤ ∫ g.
  • Estimate of the integral: m(b-a) ≤ ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M(b-a), where m and M are the minimum and maximum of f on [a,b].
Mean value theorem:

If f is continuous on [a,b], then there exists c ∈ [a,b] such that ∫_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b-a).

topics.title: Newton-Leibniz formula
topics.content:
Newton-Leibniz formula:

If F is an antiderivative of f on [a,b], then
∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).

Relationship between definite and indefinite integrals:

the definite integral of a continuous function can be evaluated using any antiderivative.

Integral with a variable upper limit:

Φ(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt is an antiderivative of f (Barrow's theorem).

Applications:

computing areas, volumes, arc lengths, work done by a variable force, and other quantities.

topics.title: Substitution and integration by parts in definite integrals
topics.content:
Substitution:

If x = φ(t) is continuously differentiable on [α,β], φ(α)=a, φ(β)=b, then
∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_α^β f(φ(t)) φ'(t) dt.

Integration by parts:

∫_a^b u dv = u v |_a^b - ∫_a^b v du.

Examples:
  • ∫_0^π x sin x dx = [ -x cos x ]_0^π + ∫_0^π cos x dx = ...
  • ∫_0^1 e^x dx = e^1 - e^0 = e-1.

When applying substitution, the limits of integration must be changed accordingly.

topics.title: Improper integrals
topics.content:
Improper integrals of the first kind

(infinite limits):
∫_a^∞ f(x) dx = lim_{b→∞} ∫_a^b f(x) dx, if the limit exists (converges). Similarly for ∫_{-∞}^b and ∫_{-∞}^∞.

Improper integrals of the second kind

(unbounded function):
If f is unbounded near a point c ∈ [a,b], the integral is defined as the limit of integrals over intervals from which a neighbourhood of c is removed.

Convergence tests:
  • Comparison with standard integrals: ∫_1^∞ dx/x^p converges if p>1, diverges if p≤1; ∫_0^1 dx/x^p converges if p<1, diverges if p≥1.
  • Limit comparison test: if f(x) ∼ g(x) as x→∞ (or near a singularity), then the integrals behave in the same way.
Absolute and conditional convergence:
  • An integral is absolutely convergent if ∫ |f| converges.
  • It is conditionally convergent if it converges but not absolutely (e.g., ∫ sin x/x dx).

topics.title: Applications of the definite integral
topics.content:
Area of a plane region:
  • In Cartesian coordinates: S = ∫_a^b |f(x)-g(x)| dx.
  • In polar coordinates: S = ½ ∫_α^β r(φ)² dφ.
Volume of a solid of revolution:
  • Around the x‑axis: V = π ∫_a^b f(x)² dx.
  • Around the y‑axis (cylindrical shell method): V = 2π ∫_a^b x f(x) dx.
Arc length of a curve:
  • In Cartesian coordinates: L = ∫_a^b √(1 + (f'(x))²) dx.
  • Parametric form: L = ∫_α^β √(x'(t)² + y'(t)²) dt.
Surface area of revolution:

S = 2π ∫_a^b f(x) √(1 + (f'(x))²) dx.

Physical applications:
  • Work done by a variable force: A = ∫_a^b F(x) dx.
  • Mass of a rod with variable density ρ(x): m = ∫_a^b ρ(x) dx.
  • Centre of mass coordinates: x_c = (∫ x ρ(x) dx) / m, similarly for y.
  • Moments of inertia.

topics.title: First‑order differential equations
topics.content:
Basic concepts:

An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates the independent variable x, the unknown function y(x) and its derivatives. The order is the highest derivative present. A solution is a function y(x) satisfying the equation. The Cauchy problem consists in finding a solution that satisfies an initial condition y(x0) = y0.

Existence and uniqueness theorem (Picard–Lindelöf):

under certain conditions, the solution of the Cauchy problem exists and is unique.

Types of equations integrable in quadratures:
  • Separable equations: y' = f(x)g(y). Solution: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, then integrate.
  • Homogeneous equations: y' = f(y/x). Substitute u = y/x, y' = u + x u' to obtain a separable equation.
  • Linear equations: y' + p(x)y = q(x). Solve using an integrating factor μ = e^{∫ p dx}. Then (μ y)' = μ q, hence y = (1/μ)∫ μ q dx + C/μ.
  • Bernoulli equation: y' + p(x)y = q(x) y^n (n≠0,1). Substitute z = y^{1-n} to reduce it to a linear equation.
  • Exact differential equations: M(x,y) dx + N(x,y) dy = 0, where ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x. Then there exists a function U(x,y) such that dU = M dx + N dy, and the solution is U(x,y) = C. If the condition is not satisfied, we can look for an integrating factor.

topics.title: Higher‑order differential equations
topics.content:
Reduction of order:
  • Equation does not contain y explicitly: F(x, y', y'') = 0. Substitute p = y' to obtain a first‑order equation.
  • Equation does not contain x explicitly: F(y, y', y'') = 0. Substitute p = y', then y'' = p dp/dy, leading to a first‑order equation in p(y).
Linear differential equations of order n:

y^{(n)} + a_1(x) y^{(n-1)} + ... + a_n(x) y = f(x).

  • Homogeneous (f=0): they satisfy the superposition principle. A fundamental system of solutions consists of n linearly independent solutions. The Wronskian W ≠ 0 for a fundamental system. The general solution is a linear combination of fundamental solutions.
  • Non‑homogeneous: general solution = general solution of the homogeneous equation + a particular solution of the non‑homogeneous equation.
  • Method of variation of parameters (Lagrange) for finding a particular solution given a fundamental system.

topics.title: Linear homogeneous equations with constant coefficients
topics.content:
Equation: y^{(n)} + a_1 y^{(n-1)} + ... + a_n y = 0, where a_i are constants.

Characteristic equation:

λ^n + a_1 λ^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0.

Construction of a fundamental system of solutions:
  • For each real simple root λ, we have a solution e^{λx}.
  • For a real root λ of multiplicity k, we have solutions e^{λx}, x e^{λx}, ..., x^{k-1} e^{λx}.
  • For a pair of simple complex conjugate roots α ± iβ, we have solutions e^{αx} cos βx, e^{αx} sin βx.
  • If a complex conjugate pair has multiplicity k, we add solutions multiplied by x, x², ..., x^{k-1} before cos and sin.

The general solution is a linear combination of all found solutions.

topics.title: Linear non‑homogeneous equations with constant coefficients
topics.content:
Equation: L[y] = f(x). General solution: y = y_h + y_p.

Method of undetermined coefficients (judicious guessing) for right‑hand sides of special form:
  • f(x) = P_m(x) e^{αx} (polynomial).
  • f(x) = e^{αx} (A cos βx + B sin βx).
  • f(x) = a sum of such products.

The particular solution is sought in a form similar to f(x), but if α or α±iβ is a root of the characteristic equation, we multiply by x^k (k is the multiplicity of the root).

Method of variation of parameters (Lagrange)

applicable for any continuous f. If a fundamental system y₁,...,y_n of the homogeneous equation is known, the particular solution is sought as y = Σ C_i(x) y_i, where C_i'(x) are found from a system obtained after substitution into the equation.

topics.title: Numerical series
topics.content:
Basic concepts:

A series is an expression of the form Σ_{n=1}^∞ a_n. The partial sums are S_n = Σ_{k=1}^n a_k. The series converges if the limit S = lim S_n exists and is finite; otherwise it diverges.

Necessary condition:

if a series converges, then a_n → 0. The converse is not true.

Series with positive terms:
  • Comparison test: if 0 ≤ a_n ≤ b_n and Σ b_n converges, then Σ a_n converges; if Σ a_n diverges, then Σ b_n diverges.
  • Limit comparison test: if lim a_n / b_n = c ∈ (0,∞), then the two series behave the same.
  • Ratio test (d'Alembert): lim a_{n+1}/a_n = l. If l<1 – converges, l>1 – diverges, l=1 – inconclusive.
  • Root test (Cauchy): lim sup √[n]{a_n} = l. Similarly.
  • Integral test (Cauchy): if a_n = f(n) with f positive and decreasing, then the series converges ⇔ ∫_1^∞ f(x) dx converges.
Standard series:
  • Geometric series Σ r^n converges if |r|<1.
  • Harmonic series Σ 1/n diverges.
  • Generalised harmonic series Σ 1/n^p converges if p>1, diverges if p≤1.

topics.title: Alternating series. Absolute and conditional convergence
topics.content:
Alternating series:

Σ (-1)^{n-1} b_n, b_n > 0.

Leibniz test:

if b_n decreases monotonically to 0, then the series converges (conditionally). Remainder estimate: |R_n| ≤ b_{n+1}.

Absolute convergence:

a series Σ a_n converges absolutely if Σ |a_n| converges. An absolutely convergent series converges.

Conditional convergence:

the series converges but not absolutely.

Properties:
  • An absolutely convergent series can be rearranged arbitrarily – the sum remains the same.
  • For a conditionally convergent series, rearrangement can yield any sum (Riemann rearrangement theorem).

topics.title: Power series
topics.content:
Definition:

A series of the form Σ c_n (x - x0)^n.

Abel's theorem:

If the power series converges at some point x ≠ x0, then it converges absolutely for |x-x0| < R and diverges for |x-x0| > R, where R is the radius of convergence. Additional investigation is required at the endpoints |x-x0| = R.

Radius of convergence:

can be found by R = 1/lim sup √[n]{|c_n|} or R = lim |c_n / c_{n+1}| (if the limit exists).

Properties:

On any closed interval inside the interval of convergence, the series converges uniformly, its sum is continuous, and the series can be integrated and differentiated term‑by‑term.

Taylor and Maclaurin series:

Expanding a function into a power series. Conditions for the function to coincide with its Taylor series.

Expansions of basic functions (Maclaurin series) have been given in the topic “Taylor's formula”.

They are used for approximate calculations and for solving differential equations.

topics.title: Introduction to Fourier series
topics.content:
Orthogonal systems of functions:

Functions φ_n(x) and ψ_m(x) are orthogonal on [a,b] if ∫ φ_n φ_m dx = 0 for n≠m. The trigonometric system {1, cos(nπx/L), sin(nπx/L)} is orthogonal on [-L, L].

Fourier series

for a function f(x) of period 2L:
f(x) ∼ a0/2 + Σ_{n=1}^∞ (a_n cos(nπx/L) + b_n sin(nπx/L)).

Fourier coefficients:

a0 = (1/L) ∫_{-L}^{L} f(x) dx,
a_n = (1/L) ∫_{-L}^{L} f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx,
b_n = (1/L) ∫_{-L}^{L} f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.

Convergence conditions:

If f is piecewise smooth, its Fourier series converges to f at points of continuity and to the average of the left‑hand and right‑hand limits at discontinuities.

Parseval's identity:

(1/L)∫_{-L}^{L} f² dx = a0²/2 + Σ (a_n² + b_n²).

Applications:

solving the heat equation, wave equation, approximation of functions.

topics.title: Functions of several variables: basic concepts
topics.content:
A function of n variables is a mapping f: D ⊂ ℝⁿ → ℝ. The domain D is the set of points where the function is defined. The graph is the set of points (x₁,...,xₙ, f(x)) in ℝⁿ⁺¹ (a surface).

Limit of a function of several variables:

We say lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that for all x in the punctured δ‑neighbourhood of a we have |f(x)-L|<ε. The Heine definition (in terms of sequences) can also be used.

Continuity:

f is continuous at a if lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a).

Properties:

Sum, product, and quotient (with non‑zero denominator) of continuous functions are continuous. Composition is continuous. On compact sets, a continuous function is bounded and attains its extremes (analogues of the Weierstrass and Cauchy theorems).

topics.title: Partial derivatives and total differential
topics.content:
Partial derivative

with respect to x:
∂f/∂x = lim_{Δx→0} (f(x+Δx, y) - f(x,y))/Δx.
Similarly for y. Geometrically, it is the rate of change along the coordinate axes.

Higher order partial derivatives:

∂²f/∂x², ∂²f/∂x∂y, etc. Clairaut's theorem: if the mixed partial derivatives are continuous, they are equal (order of differentiation does not matter).

Differentiability:

The function f(x,y) is said to be differentiable at a point if its total increment can be written as
Δf = A Δx + B Δy + o(√(Δx²+Δy²)). Then A = ∂f/∂x, B = ∂f/∂y.

Total differential:

df = (∂f/∂x) dx + (∂f/∂y) dy. The first differential is form‑invariant: if x,y themselves are functions, the same formula holds.

Tangent plane

to the surface z = f(x,y) at (x0,y0):
z - z0 = f_x(x0,y0)(x-x0) + f_y(x0,y0)(y-y0).
Normal vector: (f_x, f_y, -1).

topics.title: Directional derivative. Gradient
topics.content:
Directional derivative

for a unit vector l = (cos α, cos β):
∂f/∂l = lim_{t→0} (f(x0 + t cos α, y0 + t cos β) - f(x0,y0))/t.
It can be expressed using partial derivatives:
∂f/∂l = f_x cos α + f_y cos β.

Gradient:

grad f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y) – a vector pointing in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the function. Its magnitude is the rate of increase in that direction.

Relation:

the directional derivative in the direction l equals the dot product of the gradient with l:
∂f/∂l = (grad f)·l.

Therefore, grad f is perpendicular to the level curves.

topics.title: Extrema of functions of several variables
topics.content:
Local extremum:

A point (x0,y0) is a local maximum (minimum) if there exists a neighbourhood where f(x,y) ≤ f(x0,y0) (≥).

Necessary condition:

if a point of extremum has partial derivatives, they must be zero (stationary point).

Sufficient condition for functions of two variables:

At a stationary point (x0,y0) denote f_xx = A, f_yy = C, f_xy = B. Compute Δ = AC - B².

  • If Δ > 0 and A > 0 – local minimum.
  • If Δ > 0 and A < 0 – local maximum.
  • If Δ < 0 – saddle point (not an extremum).
  • If Δ = 0 – further analysis is required.
Constrained extremum

subject to a constraint g(x,y) = 0. Use the method of Lagrange multipliers: construct the Lagrange function L(x,y,λ) = f(x,y) + λ g(x,y), and find stationary points with respect to x,y,λ. Those points are candidates for constrained extrema.

topics.title: Multiple integrals (introduction)
topics.content:
Double integral

over a rectangular region – a generalisation of the definite integral to functions of two variables. Defined via partitions of the region into subregions, integral sums, and a limit.

Geometric meaning:

if f(x,y) ≥ 0, the double integral equals the volume of the cylindrical solid under the surface z = f(x,y).

Properties:

linearity, additivity with respect to the domain.

Reduction to iterated integrals (Fubini's theorem):

for a rectangular region [a,b]×[c,d],
∬ f(x,y) dxdy = ∫_a^b (∫_c^d f(x,y) dy) dx = ∫_c^d (∫_a^b f(x,y) dx) dy.

Change of variables:

when changing to new coordinates (u,v) with Jacobian J = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v), the formula is:
∬ f(x,y) dxdy = ∬ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) |J| du dv.

Polar coordinates:

x = r cos φ, y = r sin φ, Jacobian = r. Then ∬ f dxdy = ∬ f(r cos φ, r sin φ) r dr dφ.

Applications:

area, volume, mass of a plate with variable density, centre of mass, moments of inertia.

Triple integral

similarly for three variables. Cylindrical and spherical coordinates.
